title: Assertions
summary: Web-first assertions that retry, why fixed sleeps cause flaky tests, and soft assertions for independent checks.

lessons.title: Web-first assertions and why they retry
keyPoints: Web-first assertions (`await expect(locator)...`) retry until true or timeout.
Reading a value once with `textContent()` and then asserting is fragile.
Assert user-visible outcomes, not that an action was performed.
lessons.interviewAngle: A good interview line: "I use web-first assertions so a slow render does not cause a false failure." It shows you understand why Playwright tests are less flaky than naive scripts. If asked for an example, describe checking that an assigned pharmacist's name appears after a shift is filled.

exercises.prompt: Why is `await expect(locator).toHaveText('Filled')` more reliable than reading `textContent()` and asserting on the string?
choices: It retries until the text matches or the timeout ends
It does not need a browser
exercises.explanation: Web-first assertions poll the page; a one-time read can catch the page mid-update.

exercises.prompt: Which assertion checks that exactly four shift rows are listed?
exercises.explanation: `toHaveCount` is the web-first assertion for the number of matching elements, and it retries.

exercises.prompt: What is the default timeout, in seconds, for a Playwright `expect` assertion?
exercises.explanation: The default `expect` timeout is 5 seconds; it can be changed in config.

exercises.prompt: A shift is assigned in the UI; the list then shows the pharmacist's name in the row for shift 1042 (row has `data-testid="shift-1042"`) and a status badge reading "Filled". Write the assertions, and explain in two sentences why you wrote them as web-first assertions.
rubric: Locates the row by test id
Uses await expect with toContainText/toHaveText and toBeVisible

lessons.title: No fixed sleeps, soft assertions and polling
keyPoints: Replace `waitForTimeout` with an assertion on the real condition.
Raise a timeout on one assertion if the app is legitimately slow.
Soft assertions collect several failures in one run; use them for independent checks only.
`expect.poll` retries non-element values; `waitForResponse` waits on the network, started before the action.
lessons.interviewAngle: "How do you avoid flaky tests?" starts here. Say you wait on conditions, not time, and use retrying assertions. Be honest that you know `waitForTimeout` exists and why you avoid it, rather than claiming you never saw one. If you inherited a test with a sleep, say you replaced it with an assertion.

exercises.prompt: What is the best replacement for `await page.waitForTimeout(3000)` before checking that a status shows "Filled"?
choices: Put the check inside a try/catch and ignore failures
exercises.explanation: Assert on the condition itself; it waits only as long as needed and fails clearly if it never happens.

choices: When later steps need the earlier check to pass
When you want the test to never fail
When checking several independent facts on a page and you want all failures reported
When you need to wait for an element
exercises.explanation: Soft assertions record failures and continue, then fail the test at the end, which shows every problem in one run.

exercises.prompt: Why start `waitForResponse` before the click rather than after?
choices: The click would be ignored otherwise
The response might arrive before you start listening and be missed
exercises.explanation: If the response comes back before the listener exists, the wait would hang. Create the promise first, act, then await it.

rubric: Keeps a retrying expect on the Cancelled text
Uses expect.soft for the pharmacy name
Explains why the sleep is a problem

lessons.title: Assertions drill: pick the right one
keyPoints: `toHaveText` is a full match; `toContainText` is partial; both accept an array for lists.
`toHaveClass('x')` is a full match; use a regex when other classes may exist.
Plain `expect(value).toBe()` does not retry; use it for non-page values.
lessons.interviewAngle: A typical question: "what assertions do you use most?" Name five: toBeVisible, toHaveText, toHaveCount, toHaveURL, toBeChecked, and say they retry. Honest framing: you used a small set in basic tests; this drill widened it on a demo site. This goes beyond basic tests: say it was learned in practice on a demo site, not used at work.

exercises.prompt: The list shows exactly "Buy milk" then "Book a flight". Which assertion checks both titles in order?
exercises.explanation: An array form of toHaveText checks each matched element in order. Count alone would pass with any two titles.

exercises.prompt: An element's text is "Book a flight". What does `toHaveText('Book')` do?
choices: Passes, because the text starts with Book
Fails, because toHaveText is a full match; use toContainText for part of it
exercises.explanation: I ran it: Expected "Book", Received "Book a flight".

exercises.prompt: Which assertion checks that a checkbox is ticked? (Name only, for example toBeVisible.)
Which line is **not** a retrying web-first assertion?
exercises.explanation: It reads the count once, then does a plain comparison. If the page is still updating it can fail wrongly.

exercises.prompt: A user adds two todos, ticks the first and opens the Active filter. Write the assertions for: the URL; exactly one visible todo; the count text; that the Clear completed button still exists. State which you used toHaveText or toContainText for, and why.
rubric: URL assertion with a regex or full URL
Count text asserted with toHaveText or toContainText with a reason
